title: Rhythm From Structure: Neural Rhythm Generation, Respiratory Skeletal Evolution, and Breathing Flexibility in Hominins
content:
Rhythm emerges from structure. From the deep, diaphragm-locked ribcages of Australopithecus and Neandertals to the flat ribcage with torsioned ribs of Homo sapiens, thoracic evolution reshaped how hominins breathe: not just how fast, but how adaptive to internal and external constraints. Combined with nasal and neural evidence, this review proposes that our capacity to rapidly shift breathing rhythm during running or speech is written into the bones of the human chest.


ABSTRACT

In humans, respiratory patterns and rhythms have evolved in close association with changes in body form, locomotor behaviors, and ventilatory biomechanics. In quadrupedal mammals, breathing and locomotion are mechanically locked during running in a fixed 1:1 stride−breath coupling. The adoption of upright posture in hominins decoupled breathing from locomotion, enabling flexible coupling ratios and a wider range of ventilatory rhythms. This review integrates the neural generation of respiratory rhythms, locomotor–respiratory entrainment, and paleoanthropological evidence for skeletal changes relevant to breathing rhythm evolution. Central to this is the transformation of thoracic morphology: early hominins possessed broad, deep thoraces with low-torsion, horizontally oriented ribs and diaphragm-dominated ventilation suited to slow breathing. In modern humans, the thorax became flatter due to complex rib curvatures, structurally optimized for cooperative action between diaphragm and rib cage muscles, that is, the mechanical foundation of tachypneic flexibility in Homo sapiens. Craniofacial evidence points in the same direction: the projecting external nose of H. erectus may have reinforced slow nasal breathing as the default mode, with implications for thermoregulation and limbic neural entrainment. Together, thoracic and nasal evolution define a morpho-rhythmic continuum from early hominins as diaphragmatic slow breathers to the rhythmically flexible respiratory system of H. sapiens.
